vignette: John, a 72-year-old software engineer from North America, has lived through an experience that continues to haunt him. A survivor of torture, John struggles with the lingering effects that have reshaped his daily life and his sense of self. The trauma he endured left deep psychological scars, leading him to constantly monitor his own thoughts for signs of going crazy. He avoids being alone in a room or building and tries hard not to think about the traumatic events. These maladaptive strategies have become a part of his daily routine, driven by the overwhelming sense of threat he feels. John perceives danger around every corner, particularly in the faces and body language of others. This hyper-vigilance is evident as he studies people intently, trying to detect any signs of potential threats. His sleep has been severely disrupted as well; falling asleep is difficult because he believes he must stay alert at all times. The traumatic experience has also profoundly affected his sense of self and trust in others. John has come to believe that he acted in ways that go against who he fundamentally is, which has led him to feel deeply violated and isolated from those around him. This violation has eroded his faith in people and life itself, creating a pervasive feeling of disconnection. His negative appraisals have significantly influenced the maladaptive strategies he employs. The belief that he cannot trust others and that there is inherent danger in solitude leads him to constantly monitor his thoughts and avoid being alone. Similarly, the threat perceptions—such as the need to check doors and windows repeatedly—intensify these feelings of isolation and loss of faith. Over time, John’s maladaptive strategies have reinforced his negative appraisals. The more he monitors his own thoughts and avoids situations where he might feel vulnerable, the stronger his belief that people cannot be trusted grows. This cycle has tightened over months, making it increasingly difficult for him to engage in normal daily activities or maintain meaningful relationships. John's occupation as a software engineer provides a backdrop against which these symptoms are particularly visible. He often isolates himself at work and avoids group meetings where he might feel exposed. His colleagues have noticed changes in his behavior but remain unaware of the underlying trauma. The cumulative effect of these behaviors has led to significant relational strain. John’s isolation has created a barrier between him and potential friendships, leaving him feeling more alone than ever. This sense of being set apart from others only exacerbates his feelings of distrust and constant vigilance. What finally brought John to seek help was a realization that his life had become unmanageable. He is most afraid of never recovering his sense of self and the trust he once had in people. At the same time, he hopes for relief from the relentless fear and isolation, seeking a return to some semblance of normalcy and connection with others. John's journey towards healing will require addressing both the maladaptive strategies and the underlying negative appraisals that perpetuate his sense of threat and isolation.
